student_view.objective: First flight experience, basic circuit around KHMP
must_do_actions: Complete REP preflight walk-around (interior inspection + external walk-around)
Remove wheel chocks, tiedowns, and pitot tube cover
Fly a simple circuit around KHMP on Runway 24
Takeoff at 55 KIAS, climb at 74 KIAS
Maintain pattern altitude 1,882 MSL (1,000 AGL)
Approach at 65 KIAS
Land on Runway 24
target_numbers: Preflight walk-around completion (all items checked, chocks/tiedowns/pitot cover removed)

content.summary: The airplane felt busy because pitch, power, speed, and altitude were all moving at once. You were managing everything manually — no framework, no system, just raw inputs. That's why it was hard. The controls do what you tell them, but they don't think for you.
what_you_did_well: You removed chocks, tiedowns, pitot cover, and towbar. REP walk-around complete.
You rotated near 55, climbed near 74, approached near 65. The numbers weren't perfect but you were in the range.
You kept the airport in sight and landed on the runway. First flight, gear down, no drama.
what_to_fix: Every input has a consequence. You're making big corrections when small ones would do. Small stick, small result. Big stick, big surprise.
You may have noticed the airplane pulling left during takeoff and climb. That's real. It's not a trim problem. Your feet matter as much as your hands — use rudder to track straight.
Head up. Eyes outside. Stop scanning the panel like it has the answers. The horizon is your primary instrument right now.
coach_callouts: What moved today: your hands moved the ailerons and elevator. Your feet moved the rudder. The throttle moved the power. Physical cause, physical effect. That's the entire lesson.
What you felt: pressure through the yoke, resistance in the pedals, the seat pushing back during the climb. That feedback is real data. Learn to trust it before the gauges.
What to notice next time: how the airplane tells you what it's doing before the instruments do. Vibration, pressure changes, pitch attitude shifting. Feel first, confirm on the panel second.
content.next_focus: Lesson 2 introduces the Energy Management model — the framework that calms things down. Power controls energy. Pitch distributes it. That one idea organizes everything you just did.

reveal.primary_focus: What the student just experienced on their first flight — connecting the physical sensations to the controls and forces acting on the aircraft
reveal_topics: Why Does the Airplane Climb? — Increasing angle of attack increases lift; lift exceeds weight; drag also increases requiring more thrust. The engine doesn't 'pull' the airplane up — lift does.

Angle of Attack vs. Pitch Attitude — Pitch attitude is nose position relative to horizon (what you see); angle of attack is wing angle relative to airflow (what creates lift). They are related but NOT the same.
Preview: In later lessons, fly by pitch + power combinations, not just 'pulling back to climb.'

concepts.instructional_intent: Identify all major external components and specifications of the Cessna 172S (engine, propeller, fuel capacity, weights, speeds, range)

Perform a thorough preflight inspection using checklist — interior inspection (fuel, master switch, controls, fuel selector) and external walk-around (pilot door, left wing, nose, right wing, tail, engine) with understanding of why each item matters
Explain the function of ailerons (roll), elevator (pitch), rudder (yaw), and trim tab — including common misconceptions like using rudder for steering in flight
Understand lift, weight, thrust, and drag and their equilibrium in steady level flight
Distinguish IAS, CAS, TAS, and groundspeed; understand why you fly using IAS but navigate using groundspeed
Understand 14 CFR 91.155 Class G airspace weather minimums for KHMP including visibility and cloud clearance requirements
Know field elevation (882 MSL), runway (24/06, 5,000×100 ft), CTAF (122.8 MHz), pattern altitude (1,882 MSL), left traffic, and standard traffic pattern radio calls

student_view.objective: Learn flaps and trim; fly 3 complete traffic patterns with configuration management
must_do_actions: Fly 3 complete traffic patterns on Runway 24
Deploy flaps incrementally: 0° (takeoff) → 10° (downwind) → 20° (base) → 30° (final)
Use trim to relieve yoke pressure at each configuration change
Maintain downwind speed 90 KIAS
Maintain approach speed 65 KIAS
Execute go-around if landing is unstable (full power, flaps 20°, climb at 74 KIAS)
Perform at least one go-around as part of GTGL sequence
target_numbers: Flap deployment at correct pattern legs (10° downwind, 20° base, 30° final)
Trim usage after each configuration change
Go-around execution (full power, correct flap management, climb at 74 KIAS)

content.summary: Power = Energy. Pitch = Distribution. That's the model. Everything you did today — climbs, descents, the go-around, the pattern — was an energy transaction. Configuring early with flaps and trim made the final approach stable. Final is for aiming, not fixing.
what_you_did_well: You used power changes to manage total energy state. Add power = more energy. Reduce power = less. You saw the relationship in the climb and descent.
You executed the go-around. That's not a failure — it's an energy state transition from low to high. Full power, pitch up, flaps incremental, climb away.
You trimmed for hands-off flight on downwind. That's workload reduction — managing energy instead of fighting the yoke.
what_to_fix: Ball centered in the climb. This is graded. You felt the left-turning tendencies during every climb — P-factor, torque, spiraling slipstream, gyroscopic precession. All four push you left when power is high. Right rudder. Check the ball.
Stop chasing airspeed with the throttle. Power sets total energy. Pitch distributes it. If you're slow and level, pitch down — don't add power unless you need to change the total energy state.
Configure earlier. Flaps 10 abeam, flaps 20 on base, flaps 30 on final. Late configuration means you're fixing on final instead of aiming.
coach_callouts: Power = Energy. Pitch = Distribution. Say it until it's automatic. This is the framework for everything from here forward.

The go-around proved the model. You were in a low-energy state on approach. Full power injected maximum energy. Pitch directed it upward. That's not an emergency — that's energy management working exactly as designed.
You compensated for left-turning tendencies with right rudder during every climb. That compensation becomes more critical at the edges of the envelope. The ball tells you everything.
content.next_focus: Lesson 3 shows you where the edges are — and why the airplane behaves differently near them. Same energy model, but now you'll feel what happens when energy runs low and when load runs high.

reveal.primary_focus: How flaps changed the airplane's behavior in the pattern — connecting the physical sensation of slowing down when flaps are deployed to the aerodynamics
reveal_topics: Why Flaps Create Drag — Parasitic drag increases exponentially with flap deflection; disrupts smooth airflow, creates turbulent wake, forms pressure differential behind flap.
Induced drag actually decreases slightly because flaps increase lift coefficient, reducing angle of attack needed for same lift.
Net Effect: Total drag increases significantly, allowing steeper descents at slower airspeeds.
Advanced Concept: Flaps don't make you descend — they allow you to descend without accelerating. Without power reduction, airplane slows but temporarily maintains altitude.

concepts.instructional_intent: Explain flap settings (0°/10°/20°/30°/40°), aerodynamic effects (increased lift, increased drag, decreased stall speed), and deployment speeds (VFE 110 KIAS)
Teach correct trim technique — establish pitch with yoke first, then trim to zero pressure. Address common mistake of flying with trim instead of yoke.
Foundational concept: pitch controls airspeed, power controls altitude. Provide combinations for maintaining altitude, climbing, and descending at constant airspeed.
Standard left traffic for Runway 24 — segment profiles for takeoff, crosswind, downwind, base, and final including altitude, airspeed, flap setting, and power setting for each leg
Explain density altitude concept, calculation method (pressure altitude + temperature correction), and its impact on takeoff roll, climb rate, and landing distance

When to go around (unstable approach, misalignment, excessive sink rate, bounced landing, runway not clear). Go-around procedure: full power, carb heat off, flaps 20°, pitch for Vy 74 KIAS, incremental flap retraction. Emphasize: no shame in a go-around.

quizSeeds.question: During your Lesson 1 takeoff, the airplane became airborne at 55 KIAS. What happened at that moment?
options: Thrust exceeded drag, causing the airplane to accelerate past its structural limit
Lift generated by the wings exceeded the weight of the airplane
The engine reached maximum RPM and forced the airplane off the ground
Drag decreased to zero, allowing the airplane to float
quizSeeds.explanation: At rotation speed, the wings generate enough lift to overcome the airplane's weight. The airplane flies because lift > weight.

quizSeeds.question: On downwind during Lesson 1, the airplane maintained level flight at a constant altitude and airspeed. Which statement best describes the four forces?
options: Thrust is greater than drag, and lift is greater than weight
Thrust equals drag, and lift equals weight — all four forces are in equilibrium
Only lift and weight are acting; thrust and drag are negligible at pattern speed
Drag is greater than thrust, but lift compensates by increasing
quizSeeds.explanation: In unaccelerated, level flight at constant speed, all four forces are balanced: thrust = drag, lift = weight.

quizSeeds.question: When you reduced power on your Lesson 1 approach, the nose dropped and the airplane began descending. Why?
options: Reducing power caused the wings to stall immediately
The airplane's weight shifted forward when the throttle was pulled back
Less power meant less thrust, which meant less speed, which meant less lift — weight began exceeding lift
Drag increased when the throttle was reduced, pushing the nose down
quizSeeds.explanation: Reducing power starts a chain: less thrust → airplane decelerates → less airflow over wings → less lift → weight wins → airplane descends.

quizSeeds.question: Which force directly opposes the forward motion of the airplane through the air?
quizSeeds.explanation: Drag is the aerodynamic resistance that opposes the airplane's motion through the air.

quizSeeds.question: During your Lesson 1 climb after takeoff, thrust was greater than drag. What was the relationship between lift and weight?
options: Lift was less than weight — the airplane was sinking while climbing
Lift was equal to weight — the airplane was in equilibrium
Lift had an upward component exceeding weight, allowing altitude gain
Weight was zero during the climb because the airplane was airborne
quizSeeds.explanation: During a climb, the lift vector has a vertical component exceeding weight, allowing the airplane to gain altitude.

student_view.objective: Explore the edges of the flight envelope: slow flight, power-off stalls, and steep turns at 3,500 MSL
must_do_actions: Climb to 3,500 MSL (safety altitude, 2,618 AGL)
Perform slow flight at 50-55 KIAS (5-10 knots above stall)
Execute power-off stall and recovery (PARE: Pitch down, Add power, Rudder, Elevator)
Perform steep turns at 45° bank (±5°)
Maintain altitude ±100 feet, heading ±10° during slow flight
Maintain altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots during steep turns
Know best glide speed: 68 KIAS
target_numbers: Slow flight: airspeed 50-55 KIAS, altitude ±100 ft, heading ±10°
Power-off stall: recognition and recovery using PARE
Steep turns: 45° bank ±5°, altitude ±100 ft, airspeed ±10 knots, rollout ±10° of entry heading
Safety altitude adherence (recovery by 2,500 MSL minimum)

content.summary: Slow flight and stalls are the low-energy boundary of the flight envelope. Steep turns are the high-load boundary. They are connected — not separate maneuvers. You explored both edges today. The airplane behaves differently near its limits, and now you know what that looks and feels like.
what_you_did_well: You held slow flight at the low-energy boundary without panicking. Buffet, mushy controls, high nose attitude — you recognized the signals.
Stall recovery sequence was correct: reduce AoA, full power, level wings, climb. The wing exceeds critical angle of attack — recovery is always the same.
In steep turns you felt the load factor increase. Back-pressure to hold altitude, stall speed rising to ~57 KIAS at 45° bank. That's you feeling the envelope shrink.
what_to_fix: Stall recovery needs to be faster. Reduce AoA and add full power simultaneously, not sequentially. Every second of delay costs altitude you don't have at the boundary.
In steep turns, the safe envelope shrinks. Load factor increases, stall speed rises. You're losing altitude because you're not adding enough back-pressure to compensate. Respect the boundary.
Left-turning tendencies are most pronounced at high power, low speed, and high AoA — exactly where you were operating today. Right rudder compensates. The ball confirms. Don't forget it at the edges.
coach_callouts: Slow flight is not a maneuver you practice and forget. It's the low-energy boundary. The airplane is almost out of margin. A stall is what happens when you cross that boundary — the wing exceeds critical angle and lift collapses.

Steep turns are the high-load boundary. At 45° bank, load factor is ~1.41G and stall speed jumps 19%. The low-energy edge moved closer to you. Pulling harder when already slow pushes you toward a boundary that's already closer than normal.
These edges are connected through energy. That's the point. Envelope awareness is not a list of maneuvers — it's understanding where you are relative to the boundaries at all times.
content.next_focus: Lesson 4 is your Arc 1 Check Flight. Five touch-and-goes, an emergency landing on Rwy 06, and no coaching. You'll link everything under pressure. The Theory Reveal in the debrief will connect all three mental models.

reveal.primary_focus: What the airplane felt like near its limits — connecting the physical sensations (buffet, mushy controls, increased G-force) to the aerodynamic principles
reveal_topics: The Backside of the Power Curve — At very slow airspeeds (<65 KIAS in C172), induced drag dominates. To fly slower, you need more power (not less). This is 'Region of Reversed Command.'
On final approach at 65 KIAS, you're near the backside. If you correct high sink rate with elevator only (pulling back), you slow into reversed command region — need more power.
Correct response: Add power and adjust pitch. 'Chasing airspeed with pitch' on approach is dangerous.

Advanced Concept: The stall horn is a 'high angle of attack' warning, not a 'low airspeed' warning. You can trigger it at 90 KIAS in a 60° bank turn because load factor increases the effective weight.

concepts.concept_name: Angle of Attack and the Stall
concepts.instructional_intent: Critical concept: stalls are caused by exceeding the critical angle of attack (~16-18°), not low airspeed. A stall can occur at any airspeed, any altitude, any attitude. Cover stall warning signs (buffet, mushy controls, stall horn, high deck angle) and PARE recovery.

concepts.concept_name: Slow Flight: Controlled Flight at Minimum Airspeed
concepts.instructional_intent: Learn to recognize and operate near stall speed — high angle of attack, high induced drag, sluggish controls. ACS standards: airspeed 50-55 KIAS, altitude ±100 ft, heading ±10°. Common mistakes: maintaining altitude with elevator (secondary stall), over-banking, fixating on airspeed.

Simulates poorly executed go-around or stretching a glide. Most dangerous phase is approach to landing. Critical lesson: never stretch a glide with elevator. Include spin awareness — uncoordinated flight + stall = incipient spin.

concepts.concept_name: Steep Turns: Load Factor and Energy Management
concepts.instructional_intent: ACS: 45° bank ±5°, altitude ±100 ft, airspeed ±10 knots, rollout ±10°. Load factor at 45° = 1.41G, stall speed increases 19%. Must increase back pressure and add ~200 RPM to compensate. Energy management: potential energy (altitude) + kinetic energy (airspeed).

concepts.concept_name: Best Glide Speed and Emergency Planning
concepts.instructional_intent: Best glide speed 68 KIAS provides maximum L/D ratio. Glide ratio ~9:1 (1.5 NM per 1,000 ft AGL). Emergency landing procedure: airspeed, landing site, restart attempt, Mayday 121.5, secure aircraft. FAA NTSB 830 reporting requirements.

study_resources: AC 61-67C: Stall and Spin Awareness Training

quizSeeds.question: In the Energy Management model taught in L2, what does power (throttle) primarily control?
quizSeeds.explanation: Power controls how much total energy the airplane has. Pitch distributes it between speed and altitude.

quizSeeds.question: During your L2 climb-out, you needed right rudder to keep the ball centered. Which is NOT one of the four left-turning tendencies?
quizSeeds.explanation: Adverse yaw is caused by aileron deflection, not propeller effects. The four are P-factor, torque, spiraling slipstream, and gyroscopic precession.

quizSeeds.question: According to the Energy Management model, what does pitch (yoke fore/aft) primarily control?
options: Distribution of energy between speed and altitude
quizSeeds.explanation: Pitch up = energy goes to altitude. Pitch down = energy goes to speed. Power controls total energy; pitch distributes it.

quizSeeds.question: When executing a go-around from short final, why is full power the first action?
options: Because you need maximum energy injection immediately to arrest the descent
quizSeeds.explanation: The airplane is in a low-energy state. Full power immediately begins converting that energy deficit into climb capability.

quizSeeds.question: During a go-around at full power and low airspeed, what should you expect regarding left-turning tendencies?
options: They are at maximum strength — apply right rudder and monitor the ball
Only torque is present during a go-around
Left-turning tendencies only occur during stalls
quizSeeds.explanation: Full power + low speed + high AoA = all four left-turning tendencies at maximum. Right rudder and ball monitoring are critical.

debrief.mentalModel: Unified Framework (Physical Intimacy + Energy Management + Envelope Awareness)

content.summary: Arc 1 is complete. Here's what was actually happening across the last four lessons. Physical Intimacy gave you the airplane's feel. Energy Management gave you the framework for controlling it. Envelope Awareness showed you where the boundaries are. Together: you understand the airplane as a physical machine, an energy system you manage with power and pitch, operating within a bounded envelope where the rules change near the edges.
what_you_did_well: Five touch-and-goes with consistent energy management. Power transitions were deliberate. Downwind at 90, approach at 65, climbs at 74. The numbers had purpose.
Emergency on Rwy 06: you established best glide at 68 KIAS without pulling to stretch. Energy management under pressure — you managed the energy you had instead of wishing for more.
You recognized boundary cues throughout — buffet onset, control softening, ball displacement during power changes. Physical intimacy in action.
what_to_fix: Ball discipline during power transitions. You know the four left-turning tendencies exist. Anticipate them — lead with rudder when you add power, don't wait for the yaw to start.
Stall recovery altitude loss is still too high. Faster on the power, crisper on the pitch reduction. The energy deficit at the low-energy boundary costs altitude every second you delay.
Steep turn rollout: you're overshooting heading by 10–15°. Lead the rollout by half your bank angle. At 45° bank, start rolling wings level 20–25° before your target heading.
coach_callouts: Theory Reveal: L1 was Physical Intimacy — the airplane responds to your inputs. That's the foundation. You can't manage what you can't feel. L2 was Energy Management — Power = Energy, Pitch = Distribution. That's the operating system. L3 was Envelope Awareness — you learned where the edges are and what boundary behavior feels like. These three models stack. Feel it. Manage it. Know the limits.

Every maneuver you've flown is a combination of these three models. A climb is an energy decision with physical feedback at a point inside the envelope. A stall is a boundary crossing with physical cues you were trained to recognize. Nothing is isolated.
This framework doesn't change. It scales. Every new maneuver, every new phase, same three lenses. The complexity increases. The models don't.
content.next_focus: Arc 2: Pattern Master. These three models go into the traffic pattern at KHMP. Elevation 882 MSL, pattern altitude 1,882 MSL, downwind at 90, approach at 65. The environment gets more structured. The decisions get faster. Energy management becomes real-time. Same models, higher tempo.

reveal.primary_focus: Why the student's decision to land on Runway 06 (instead of turning back) was correct — demonstrating good Aeronautical Decision Making
reveal_topics: The Impossible Turn — Altitude loss in 180° turn: standard rate turn = 60 sec, descent ~600 FPM = 600 ft lost best case. Realistic: 800-1,000 ft due to tighter turn, higher bank/stall speed, stress/panic.
Conclusion: Unless at least 1,000 AGL, turning back is extremely dangerous.
NTSB Data: Turnback attempts after engine failure account for ~20% of fatal GA accidents — pilots underestimate altitude loss and stall/spin during the turn.

Advanced Concept: The Impossible Turn is only impossible due to poor training. If practiced at altitude (know your aircraft's turnback altitude), it can be done safely. Without practice, always land straight ahead.

concepts.instructional_intent: Assess risk using PAVE: Pilot (IMSAFE, alcohol 8-hr rule per 14 CFR 91.17), Aircraft (airworthiness, equipment ATOMATOFLAMES + FLAPS, fuel, W&B, maintenance), enVironment (weather, terrain, airport), External Pressures (passengers, boss, get-home-itis). If ≥2 high-risk items → delay; if ≥1 critical → cancel.

Day VFR required instruments (Airspeed, Tachometer, Oil pressure, Manifold pressure, Altimeter, Temperature, Oil temp, Fuel gauge, Landing gear indicator, Anti-collision lights, Magnetic compass, ELT, Safety belts). Night additions (Fuses, Landing light, Anti-collision, Position lights, Source of power). 90-day currency for passengers.

Landing → nosewheel touches → full power → flaps to 10° → verify airspeed → rotate 55 KIAS → climb 74 KIAS → retract remaining flaps after positive rate. Common mistakes: power before nosewheel, retracting all flaps at once, not verifying positive rate. When NOT to do T&Gs.

Engine failure at 300 AGL: Can NOT turn back to Runway 24. FAA guidance: below 500 AGL land straight ahead ±30°. KHMP-specific: Runway 06 is directly ahead. Procedure: best glide 68 KIAS, identify Runway 06, slight turn to align, no restart attempt (insufficient altitude), flaps as needed, land full stop.

New pilots should set higher personal minimums than FAA regulatory minimums (suggested: ceiling 3,000 AGL, vis 5 SM, wind 10 kt, crosswind 5 kt, temp above 0°C). Go/no-go framework: review METAR/TAF, check PAVE, compare to personal minimums, if any doubt → don't go. Includes METAR analysis example.

quizSeeds.question: What is the primary cause of a wing stall?
options: Exceeding the critical angle of attack
quizSeeds.explanation: A stall occurs when AoA exceeds the critical angle (~16°). Airflow separates and lift collapses.

quizSeeds.question: At 45° bank angle, the load factor is approximately 1.41G. What does this mean for stall speed?
quizSeeds.explanation: Higher load factor demands more lift from the wing. The wing must reach a higher AoA sooner, so stall speed increases ~19%.

quizSeeds.question: During stall recovery, why is right rudder especially critical when you add full power?
options: Full power at high AoA activates all four left-turning tendencies simultaneously
Right rudder prevents the engine from overheating
The rudder controls angle of attack
quizSeeds.explanation: Stall recovery puts you at high AoA with full power — P-factor, torque, slipstream, and precession all yaw the airplane left.

quizSeeds.question: In the flight envelope model, what do slow flight and stalls represent?
options: The low-energy boundary of the flight envelope
quizSeeds.explanation: Slow flight approaches the low-energy edge of the envelope. A stall crosses it.

quizSeeds.question: Why is pulling harder in a steep turn when already slow dangerous?
options: It increases AoA toward the critical angle while load factor has already raised the stall speed
quizSeeds.explanation: Higher bank = higher load factor = higher stall speed. Pulling harder increases AoA toward the already-closer stall boundary. This is the recipe for an accelerated stall or spin.

student_view.objective: Crosswind landings using crab and slip techniques with winds from 200° at 10 knots
must_do_actions: Calculate crosswind component using clock method
Fly traffic patterns with crosswind correction
Maintain crab angle on final approach to track runway centerline
Transition from crab to side slip in the flare (~10 ft AGL)
Touch down on upwind main wheel first, then downwind wheel, then nosewheel
Apply wind correction throughout the pattern (headwind/tailwind/crosswind legs)
target_numbers: Crab angle maintenance on final approach (runway centerline tracking)
Wind correction applied on all pattern legs

reveal.primary_focus: How crosswind correction felt in the airplane — connecting the physical inputs (aileron into wind, opposite rudder) to the aerodynamic forces at play
reveal_topics: Why Crosswinds Are Dangerous — The danger isn't the landing itself, it's loss of directional control after touchdown.
Side load on landing gear → potential collapse. Weathervaning: vertical stabilizer acts like weather vane, crosswind pushes tail, nose turns into wind uncontrollably.
Critical period: 0-5 seconds after touchdown (still high speed, limited rudder authority).

Advanced Concept: Maximum demonstrated crosswind is NOT a limitation — it's simply the highest crosswind tested during certification. You can legally land in higher crosswinds, but it requires exceptional skill.

concepts.instructional_intent: Understand True Course, True Heading, Wind Correction Angle, Groundspeed, and TAS. Calculate WCA using rule of thumb formula. In practice, adjust crab visually to track centerline.
Maximum demonstrated crosswind for C172S: 15 knots. Clock method: 0° = 0%, 30° = 50%, 45° = 70%, 60° = 90%, 90° = 100%. Apply to determine crosswind component and assess within limits.

Two methods: Crab (point nose into wind on final) and Slip (lower upwind wing, opposite rudder to align nose). Combined standard technique: crab on final → transition to slip in flare → land on upwind wheel first.

Forward slip: lose altitude without increasing airspeed (clear obstacles). Side slip: track runway centerline in crosswind. Both are cross-controlled states (aileron and rudder in opposite directions).

How wind affects each pattern leg: headwind on final (slower GS, steeper descent), tailwind on upwind (faster GS, shallower climb), crosswind on crosswind/base legs (drift compensation, early/late turn adjustments).

student_view.objective: Precision pattern work: ±50 feet altitude, ±5 knots airspeed, ±5° heading throughout the traffic pattern
must_do_actions: Fly traffic patterns with precision tolerances
Maintain downwind at 1,882 MSL ±50 ft, 90 KIAS ±5 knots
Maintain base at 70 KIAS ±5 knots
Maintain final at 65 KIAS ±5 knots
Use continuous trim to nail target numbers
Execute systematic instrument scan (attitude, airspeed, altitude)
Anticipate power/pitch changes at pattern transitions (abeam numbers, turning base, turning final)
target_numbers: Airspeed maintenance: downwind 90 ±5, base 70 ±5, final 65 ±5 KIAS

reveal.primary_focus: How trim and anticipation made the pattern smoother — connecting the precision numbers to the feeling of a stabilized approach
reveal_topics: Why VASI/PAPI Use 3° Glidepath — Optimized for obstacle clearance (20:1 ratio), energy management (descent at approach speed without excess power), and comfort (~300-500 FPM descent).
Math: 3° = 318 FPM per 60 knots GS. At 65 KIAS: ~345 FPM.
Shallower (2°): risk of landing long. Steeper (4°): high descent rate, hard landing.
Advanced Concept: Aircraft with higher approach speeds use the same 3° glidepath but higher descent rates (jets at 120 knots = ~640 FPM).

concepts.instructional_intent: Primary instruments by phase (level flight, climb, descent, turn). Radial scan pattern centered on attitude indicator. Avoid fixation (staring at one instrument). Scan rate ~1-2 seconds per instrument.

Correct technique: set power → adjust pitch for target airspeed → trim to zero pressure → hands-off test (should hold ±2 knots). Common mistakes: using trim to change pitch, not re-trimming after config changes, chasing trim.

Memorize power/pitch/flap settings per leg: Upwind (2,500 RPM, 0°, +7°), Crosswind (2,500, 0°, +7°), Downwind (2,300, 10°, level), Base (1,700, 20°, -3°), Final (1,500, 30°, -4°). Anticipating transitions abeam numbers, turning base, turning final.

VASI: Red/White = on glidepath, White/White = high, Red/Red = low. PAPI: 4-light system, 2 white 2 red = on glidepath. KHMP has no VASI/PAPI — use visual references (aim point stationary in windscreen).
Three standard entries: straight-in (from south, join final 2+ mi out), 45° entry to downwind (most common, Arc 2 standard), overhead break (not used in C172). Proper radio announcements for each.

student_view.objective: Arc 2 proficiency check: 5 solo (simulated) patterns with professional radio communications and precise airspeeds/landings
must_do_actions: Fly 5 traffic patterns solo (simulated)
Make professional radio calls at all required positions (entering pattern, downwind, base, final, clear of runway)
Maintain precise airspeeds throughout pattern
Execute smooth, consistent landings
Demonstrate right-of-way awareness and pattern traffic management
Handle pattern conflicts (extending downwind, going around if needed)
target_numbers: CTAF radio call accuracy and timing
Pattern precision (airspeed, altitude, heading per L6 standards)

reveal.primary_focus: Quality of radio calls and pattern discipline — connecting professional communication to safety in a busy traffic environment
reveal_topics: Why Most Accidents Happen in the Pattern — ~50% of GA accidents occur during takeoff/landing. Reasons: low altitude (no recovery margin), high workload (config, radio, traffic, airspeed), visual illusions (base-to-final overshoot, wide downwind, narrow runway), task saturation.
Mitigation: Stabilized approach criteria (if not stable by 500 AGL → go around), sterile cockpit (no non-essential talk below 1,000 AGL), callouts ('Airspeed alive', 'On speed', 'On glidepath').
Advanced Concept: Airlines use Stabilized Approach Criteria (500 AGL: on speed, on glidepath, on centerline, landing config, <1,000 FPM). If not met → mandatory go-around. Adopt this discipline.

concepts.instructional_intent: CTAF 122.8 at KHMP. When to make calls (10 mi out, entering pattern, downwind, base, final, clear of runway). Call structure: who you're calling, who you are, where you are, intentions, repeat airport. Pro tips: brief calls, phonetic alphabet, listen before transmitting.

Priority order: distress, balloons, gliders, airships, powered aircraft. Head-on: both turn right. Converging: right has right-of-way. Overtaking: pass to right. Landing: lower aircraft has priority. Pattern conflict examples.

Required training areas, proficiency demonstration, endorsements (pre-solo training 61.87(c), pre-solo knowledge test 61.87(b), solo flight). Solo limitations: make/model, daytime, 25 NM, no passengers, no compensation. Student solo accident rate ~2x higher than dual.

Spacing: 1-mile on final. Sequencing priority: final > base > downwind. Extend downwind or go around if too close. Non-standard patterns (right traffic, straight-in, helicopter). Conflict resolution examples.

Radio fails in pattern: squawk 7600, watch for light gun signals (if towered), make standard pattern, land. Light gun signal meanings (steady/flashing green, red, white; alternating red/green). Not applicable at KHMP (untowered) but required knowledge for checkride.

student_view.objective: Track VOR radials, intercept courses, and identify station passage using Providence VOR (PVD)
must_do_actions: Tune and identify Providence VOR (PVD)
Track VOR radials inbound and outbound
Intercept assigned VOR courses (30-45° intercept angle)
Identify station passage (TO/FROM flag reversal)
Maintain needle centered with small corrections (5-10°)
Perform VOR accuracy check
target_numbers: Course intercept technique (proper angle and timing)

reveal.primary_focus: How VOR tracking felt in practice — the relationship between needle deflection, heading corrections, and wind drift
reveal_topics: Why VOR Is Dying — GPS has made VOR nearly obsolete. VOR disadvantages: ground-based/line-of-sight, limited accuracy (±2° = ±2 NM at 60 NM), expensive ($100K+/year per station).
GPS advantages: satellite-based (anywhere), precise (±30 ft), cheap (no ground infrastructure).
FAA MON (Minimum Operational Network): reducing from ~1,000 to ~300 VORs by 2030, keeping essential VORs for GPS backup.
Why learn VOR? Backup if GPS fails, understanding radio nav principles (ILS, ADF, DME), required for Private Pilot checkride.
Advanced Concept: Modern aircraft use RNAV (GPS) instead of VOR — fly direct to GPS waypoints. VOR skills are still foundational for spatial awareness.

concepts.instructional_intent: VHF Omnidirectional Range (108.0-117.95 MHz). Transmits reference and variable signals; aircraft receiver compares phase difference = magnetic bearing FROM station. Components: CDI, OBS, TO/FROM indicator.

Radial = magnetic bearing FROM a VOR station. Intercept technique: set OBS, observe CDI/TO-FROM, turn to intercept at 30-45°, center needle, track with small corrections. If needle drifts right → turn right.

CDI sensitivity: each dot ≈ 2° deviation, full deflection ≈ 10°. Interpret combinations of OBS setting, TO/FROM flag, and CDI position to determine position relative to VOR. Common mistakes: chasing the needle, ignoring TO/FROM flag, not accounting for wind.
IFR: VOR checked within 30 days. Four methods: VOT (±4°), ground checkpoint (±4°), airborne checkpoint (±6°), dual VOR check (≤4° difference). VFR: no requirement but good practice.
Three classes: Terminal (1,000-12,000 AGL, 25 NM), Low (1,000-18,000 AGL, 40 NM), High (1,000-60,000 AGL, 40-130 NM). PVD is Class H. Limitations: line-of-sight, mountains, beyond radius.

student_view.objective: Navigate from KHMP to a visual checkpoint (water tower 15 NM northwest) using only chart, compass, and timer — no GPS
must_do_actions: Plot course on sectional chart using plotter
Calculate magnetic heading with wind correction (E6B or digital)
Calculate time en route using time-speed-distance formula
Fly heading, start timer at departure
Identify visual checkpoint at calculated time
Use pilotage (chart-to-ground) at checkpoints every 10-15 NM to verify position
Navigate without GPS
target_numbers: Course plotting accuracy on sectional chart
Heading calculation accuracy (wind correction, magnetic variation)
No GPS usage during navigation exercise

reveal.primary_focus: How well the dead reckoning calculations matched reality — comparing predicted vs. actual checkpoint arrival, and the importance of visual verification
reveal_topics: Why GPS Made Pilots Worse Navigators — Before GPS, pilots studied charts, understood wind, maintained situational awareness. With GPS: 'direct-to' button replaces route planning, magenta line replaces chart reading, ETA countdown replaces mental math.
NTSB Case (2018): Pilot depended entirely on GPS, GPS failed due to military jamming, pilot disoriented, ran out of fuel, fatal crash.
Lesson: Always have backup nav plan (chart, compass, checkpoints).
Advanced Concept: Modern autopilots fly GPS routes perfectly, but if you don't monitor, you won't notice when GPS drifts or fails. Trust but verify.

concepts.instructional_intent: Airport symbols (magenta = uncontrolled, blue = controlled), airspace markings, terrain (contour lines, spot elevations, obstacles), VFR checkpoints (water towers, bridges, stadiums, power plants, lakes/rivers).

Plotter = protractor + ruler. Measuring course: draw line, align plotter edge, read magnetic course at nearest meridian. Measuring distance: align scale, count NM (1 NM = 1 minute of latitude = 6,076 ft).

Heading types: TC → TH (wind correction) → MH (magnetic variation) → CH (compass deviation). Magnetic variation: 14°W at KHMP ('West is best' = add westerly variation). Use E6B for wind correction angle.
Formulas: Distance = Speed × Time, Time = Distance / Speed. E6B usage for TSD calculations. Example: 15 NM at 100 knots GS = 9 minutes.

Navigate by course, speed, time, and wind estimates. Process: plot course, calculate heading, calculate time, fly heading with timer, look for checkpoint, update position. Accuracy: ±5° heading error over 30 NM ≈ 2.5 NM off course. Pilotage + DR = robust VFR navigation.

student_view.objective: Cross-country flight to practice area (20 NM northwest) and return to KHMP with full flight planning, weather briefing, and weight & balance
must_do_actions: Complete VFR flight plan (FAA Form 7233-1)
Obtain and interpret weather briefing (METAR, TAF, NOTAMs)
Calculate weight & balance for the flight
Navigate to practice area and return
Conduct maneuvers in practice area
Close flight plan within 30 minutes of ETA
target_numbers: Flight plan closure within 30 minutes of ETA

reveal.primary_focus: Quality of flight planning process — how accurate were the weather, navigation, and W&B calculations compared to actual flight conditions
reveal_topics: Why Weight & Balance Killed So Many Pilots — NTSB Case (2019, Cessna 182): 300 lbs over gross, hot day, short runway → couldn't climb, hit trees, 4 fatalities.
Aft CG Danger: elevator may not have enough authority to recover from stall → unrecoverable stall → flat spin → fatal crash (2015 Piper Cherokee case).
Lesson: NEVER skip W&B. If over gross or out of CG → REMOVE WEIGHT.
Advanced Concept: Fuel burn shifts CG. If you start with forward CG and burn fuel, CG moves aft. Plan for most critical W&B (usually landing weight, aft CG).

concepts.instructional_intent: When required (not required for VFR but recommended >50 NM). How to file (1800wxbrief.com, phone, radio). All 15 flight plan fields explained. Critical: must close within 30 minutes of ETA or SAR initiated.

Three types: Standard (comprehensive, >6 hr from departure), Abbreviated (update), Outlook (>6 hr future). Standard briefing contents: adverse conditions, synopsis, current conditions (METARs), en route forecast, destination forecast (TAF), NOTAMs, winds aloft.
Full decode of METAR components: station, date/time, wind, visibility, sky condition, temp/dewpoint, altimeter, remarks. Example: KHMP 101735Z 24008KT 10SM FEW045 SCT250 22/14 A2990 RMK AO2.
Terminal Aerodrome Forecast decoding: validity period, wind/vis/sky groups, FROM groups (FM), TEMPO groups, BECMG groups. Interpret forecast changes and temporary conditions.
Three types: NOTAM(D), FDC NOTAM, Pointer NOTAM. Decode format. Assess impact on flight (e.g., VOR outage, runway closure, TFR).

Why it matters: overweight (longer takeoff, reduced climb, higher stall speed), aft CG (reduced stability, uncontrollable pitch-up), forward CG (higher stall speed). Cessna 172S limits: 2,550 lbs max, CG 35.0-47.3 in. Sample W&B calculation method.

student_view.objective: Handle simulated system failures: electrical failure (alternator offline), partial panel (vacuum failure), and engine roughness diagnosis
must_do_actions: Diagnose and respond to alternator failure (low voltage light, ammeter discharge)
Reduce electrical load and prioritize essential systems
Fly partial panel (no attitude indicator, no heading indicator) using turn coordinator, altimeter, airspeed, magnetic compass
Diagnose engine roughness (carburetor ice, magneto failure, fuel contamination, spark plug fouling)
Apply carb heat for suspected carb ice
Follow Aviate, Navigate, Communicate priority
Land safely at KHMP
target_numbers: Alternator failure diagnosis and load shedding
Partial panel flying proficiency (altitude ±100 ft, heading ±10°)

reveal.primary_focus: How the student handled the stress of multiple failures — connecting the physiological stress response to the importance of checklist discipline and prioritization
reveal_topics: Why 'Impossible' Emergencies Happen — Most fatal accidents aren't single failures, they're cascading failures + poor decisions.
Case (2017, Cirrus SR22): Electrical failure → pilot fixated on troubleshooting → battery died → continued into IMC → spatial disorientation → loss of control.
Lesson: Land ASAP when systems fail. Don't try to 'fix it in flight.'
Advanced Concept: Cirrus CAPS (parachute) has saved 100+ lives. If in unmanageable emergency (spin, structural failure, IMC without instruments), pull the chute. Ego kills pilots.

concepts.instructional_intent: Components: alternator (28V DC, 60A), battery (24V, ~30 min backup), voltage regulator, ammeter, circuit breakers. Normal operation vs. alternator failure. Response: reduce load, land ASAP, troubleshoot (check circuit breaker). Priority systems to keep on.

Powers gyro instruments (AI, HI/DG). Engine-driven vacuum pump, gauge (4.5-5.5 inHg normal). Failure: gauge drops to zero, AI and HI drift/tumble. Partial panel technique: pitch from airspeed, bank from turn coordinator, heading from magnetic compass (with compass errors).

Four common causes and responses: (A) Carb ice — RPM drop, rough, carb heat ON; (B) Magneto failure — sudden RPM drop, test LEFT/RIGHT, fly on good mag, land ASAP; (C) Fuel contamination — sputtering, switch tanks, fuel pump, land ASAP; (D) Spark plug fouling — rough idle, lean mixture, increase RPM.

Aviate, Navigate, Communicate. Engine failure memory items: airspeed 68 KIAS, landing site, restart (fuel/mixture/mags/primer), Mayday 121.5, secure (fuel off/mags off/master off). Bold items = memory, normal items = read when time permits.

Stress response: fight or flight, tunnel vision, auditory exclusion, cognitive narrowing. Mitigation: train until automatic, verbalize steps, prioritize (don't fixate on restart if you should be flying). DECIDE model: Detect, Estimate, Choose, Identify, Do, Evaluate.

study_resources: Cessna 172S POH: Section 3 (Emergency Procedures), Section 7 (Systems Description)

student_view.objective: Flight postponement decision — weather is below personal minimums (2,000 ft ceiling, 3 SM vis, gusts to 20 knots). Ground-only lesson studying why this weather is dangerous.
must_do_actions: Evaluate current weather conditions against personal minimums
Make go/no-go decision (correct answer: NO-GO)
Study frontal systems, thunderstorm hazards, and icing conditions
Interpret weather charts (surface analysis, prog charts, radar summary)
Re-evaluate using PAVE checklist to confirm no-go decision
target_numbers: Correct no-go decision based on weather assessment

reveal.primary_focus: Why the no-go decision was correct — reinforcing that canceling a flight IS a safe decision, not a failure
reveal_topics: Why Pilots Fly Into Weather They Shouldn't — Get-Home-Itis is the most deadly hazard in GA. Scenario: pilot at distant airport, weather deteriorating, 'I can make it', scud running, inadvertent IMC, spatial disorientation, fatal crash.
NTSB Data: ~30% of fatal GA accidents involve VFR into IMC.
Why it happens: plan continuation bias, sunk cost fallacy, social pressure, get-home-itis.
Solution: alternate transportation, no external commitments, non-negotiable personal minimums.
Advanced Concept: Airlines have 'Dispatch Authority' — dispatcher can ground a flight even if captain wants to go. As solo VFR pilot, you ARE the dispatch. Be ruthlessly conservative.

concepts.instructional_intent: Cold front (cold air displaces warm: towering cumulus, thunderstorms, rapid temp drop, winds SW→NW). Warm front (warm air overrides cold: stratus, steady rain, fog, poor vis for 100-200 NM). Occluded front (cold overtakes warm: complex mix). Stationary front (prolonged poor conditions).

Three requirements: moisture, instability, lifting. Three stages: cumulus (updrafts), mature (most dangerous, updrafts + downdrafts), dissipating. Hazards: severe turbulence, icing, hail, wind shear/microburst (4,000+ FPM), lightning. Avoidance: never penetrate embedded TS, avoid by 20 NM. If unavoidable: maneuvering speed, wings level.

Types: rime ice (freezing fog, milky white), clear ice (freezing rain, transparent, heavy), mixed (most dangerous). Occurs 0°C to -20°C in visible moisture. Effects: increased weight, disrupted airflow, higher stall speed, reduced thrust, instrument blockage. Cessna 172S NOT certified for known icing. Response: exit immediately, add power, alternate static source, declare emergency if severe.

Surface analysis (current fronts, pressure, isobars). Prog chart (forecast at 12/24/36/48 hr). Radar summary (precipitation areas, intensity, movement). Winds aloft forecast (format: 2314 = 230° at 14 kt, -04°C).

Personal minimums for student VFR: ceiling 3,000 AGL, vis 5 SM, winds <10 kt, gusts <5 kt, crosswind <5 kt, temp above freezing. Today's simulated weather fails on ceiling (2,000), visibility (3 SM), and wind gusts (20 kt). Decision: NO-GO. PAVE re-check confirms.

student_view.objective: Night pattern work (3 patterns) and lost procedures at night with reduced visual references
must_do_actions: Fly 3 traffic patterns at night
Adapt to reduced depth perception and altitude judgment
Use landing lights for depth perception near ground
Demonstrate awareness of night landing illusions
Practice lost procedures (simulated loss of visual references)
Use VOR and/or GPS 'Nearest Airport' for position recovery
target_numbers: Landing light usage for depth perception

reveal.primary_focus: How night flying changed depth perception and decision-making — what felt different compared to daytime patterns
reveal_topics: Why Night Flying Is Statistically Safer (but more dangerous in emergencies) — Night accident rate per hour is LOWER than day (less traffic, better visibility of lit airports, smoother air, more cautious pilots).
BUT: Fatal accident rate is HIGHER at night — harder to find emergency landing sites, spatial disorientation in clouds, wildlife strikes at dusk.
Lesson: Night flying is safe if proficient and prepared, but emergencies are more dangerous.
Advanced Concept: Some pilots advocate for instrument rating before extensive night flying. Rationale: night + clouds = IMC conditions, and VFR pilots aren't trained for instrument flight.

concepts.instructional_intent: Rods vs. cones: cones for color/central/bright, rods for BW/peripheral/low-light. Dark adaptation: cones ~7 min, rods ~30 min. Low oxygen reduces night vision (>5,000 MSL consider supplemental O2). Night blind spot: center of vision has no rods, look 5-10° off-center. Red cockpit lights preserve adaptation.

Featureless terrain: illusion of being higher → fly low. Bright runway lights: appear closer → fly low. Black hole approach (no lights between you and runway): no depth cues → low steep approach. Mitigation: VASI/PAPI, instruments (altimeter, VSI), consistent pattern, landing light.

Night definition: 1 hr after sunset to 1 hr before sunrise. Required (FLAPS): Fuses, Landing light (if for hire), Anti-collision lights, Position lights (nav lights: red/green/white), Source of power. Recommended: flashlight with red lens, backup battery.
14 CFR 61.57(b): to carry passengers at night, need 3 takeoffs and landings to full stop within 90 days, between 1 hr after sunset and 1 hr before sunrise, same category/class.

If uncertain of position: climb (better radio reception), circle (maintain position), contact ATC (121.5 MHz), confess ('I am a student pilot and I am lost'), squawk 7700 if critical. Use VOR to determine radial/position. GPS backup: 'Nearest Airport' function. Fuel management: don't wait until low fuel to admit lost.

student_view.objective: Comprehensive emergency scenario: simulated electrical failure at night combined with engine roughness — diagnose, prioritize, and land safely
must_do_actions: Handle simulated electrical failure at night (battery dying)
Diagnose and respond to engine roughness (suspected carb ice)
Prioritize using Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Reduce electrical load, apply carb heat
Navigate to KHMP (nearest airport) using available instruments
Declare Mayday on 121.5 MHz
Land safely with remaining battery for landing light
Apply ADM and DECIDE model throughout
target_numbers: Electrical failure management (load shedding, battery preservation)
Engine roughness diagnosis and response (carb heat)

reveal.primary_focus: How the student managed stress under compounded failures — analyzing decision quality, prioritization, and whether the accident chain was broken
reveal_topics: The 'Normalization of Deviance' — Gradual acceptance of risk because 'nothing bad happened last time.' Example: skip preflight → skip fuel sump → skip runup → miss contaminated fuel → engine quits → crash.
NASA Study: Most GA accidents involve procedural deviations that became routine.
Mitigation: checklist discipline (every flight, no shortcuts), safety culture (call out deviations), fresh eyes (have another pilot review procedures).
Advanced Concept: Airlines use Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) with no deviation tolerance. If you deviate, you debrief why. Adopt this mindset.

concepts.instructional_intent: Five hazardous attitudes (anti-authority, impulsivity, invulnerability, macho, resignation) with antidotes. DECIDE model revisited with emergency scenario application example (electrical failure: detect → estimate 30 min battery → choose land ASAP → identify nearest airport → do → evaluate).

Single failure = manageable (follow checklist). Multiple failures = overwhelming (task saturation). Prioritization (Maslow for Aviation): fly the airplane → navigate → communicate → troubleshoot (only if time permits). Apply to tonight's scenario: electrical + engine roughness + night.

Swiss Cheese Model: multiple defense layers with holes; accident occurs when holes align. Example chain: missed preflight → skipped weather brief → low fuel + headwind → press on instead of divert → fuel exhaustion. Breaking the chain: recognize multiple risk factors, act early, don't let ego/pressure drive decisions.

Progression from Arc 1 (5,000/10SM/5kt) to Arc 4 (3,000/5SM/10kt) to Private Pilot (2,000/3SM/15kt) to Instrument Pilot. Start conservative, gradually expand with proficiency, never go below FAA minimums.

After every flight: what went well, what could improve, unnecessary risks, same decisions again? Red flags: felt rushed, skipped checklist items, surprised by weather/performance, worked around problems, 'got away with that.' Log lessons, seek feedback, study accident reports.

student_view.objective: Ground-only lesson: Plan a 150 NM cross-country with 3 legs (KHMP → KBID → KACK → KHMP). No flying — complete nav log, W&B, fuel calculations, and weather brief.
must_do_actions: Plan complete 3-leg cross-country route
Prepare full navigation log (checkpoint, course, distance, altitude, TAS, wind, GS, time, fuel per leg)
Calculate fuel burn, time en route, and verify adequate fuel with 30-min reserve
Calculate weight & balance for XC flight
Select VFR cruising altitudes per 14 CFR 91.159
Identify checkpoints and alternate airports along each leg
Prepare passenger briefing (SAFETY)
Obtain simulated weather briefing

reveal.primary_focus: Quality and completeness of the flight planning package — is the student ready to execute this cross-country safely?
reveal_topics: Why Most XC Accidents Are Fuel Exhaustion — NTSB Data: ~40% of XC accidents involve fuel starvation/exhaustion. Common causes: no fuel check (assumed gauges accurate), headwind underestimate, diversion added distance, insufficient reserve, 'I can make it' syndrome.
Case (2020, Cessna 172): Planned 2.5 hr with 3 hr fuel, encountered 30-knot headwind (forecast 15), flight time 3.2 hr, ran out 5 mi from destination, forced landing in trees.
Mitigation: visual fuel check (dipstick not just gauges), conservative planning (add 50% to forecast headwind), mandatory 1-hour reserve (not 30 min), divert early.
Advanced Concept: Airlines use Minimum Fuel vs. Emergency Fuel declarations. Adopt this: if fuel gets low, declare minimum fuel early — don't wait until emergency.

concepts.instructional_intent: 14 CFR 61.1: XC for private pilot requires straight-line distance >50 NM from departure with landing at destination. Example route: KHMP → KBID (50 NM) → KACK (40 NM) → KHMP (60 NM), total 150 NM.

Complete nav log with columns: checkpoint, course (°M), distance (NM), altitude (MSL), TAS, wind, GS, time, fuel. Example filled out for Leg 1 (KHMP → KBID) with water tower and coastline checkpoints. Verify total fuel vs. available with reserve.

14 CFR 91.159: magnetic course 0-179° → odd thousands + 500 (3,500, 5,500…), 180-359° → even thousands + 500 (4,500, 6,500…). Considerations: terrain clearance (1,000 ft above highest obstacle within 4 NM), cloud clearance, density altitude, oxygen (above 12,500 for >30 min).

Identify ≥2 alternates along route (within ±10 NM, paved runway >2,500 ft, fuel if needed). Example alternates: Leg 1 KOQU/KEWB, Leg 2 KMVY, Leg 3 KPVD. Diversion criteria: weather, fuel, medical, aircraft malfunction.

SAFETY: Seatbelts, Air vents, Fire extinguisher, Exit (how to open door), Traffic (point out aircraft), You're in charge (sterile cockpit during critical phases). Additional: headset, motion sickness, questions anytime except takeoff/landing.

student_view.objective: Fly the planned XC route (KHMP → KBID → KACK → KHMP) with CFI. Expect a simulated diversion when weather at KACK deteriorates.
must_do_actions: Execute the planned cross-country flight from L15
Navigate using pilotage and dead reckoning (chart, compass, timer)
Use VOR and GPS as backup navigation aids
Handle simulated diversion from KACK to KMVY (Martha's Vineyard) due to weather
Calculate new heading, distance (~15 NM), time (~8 min), fuel (~1 gal) for diversion
Communicate diversion to ATC
Demonstrate fuel management (monitor every 15 minutes, compare to plan)
Arrive at unfamiliar airports (review Chart Supplement, CTAF, overfly to identify)

reveal.primary_focus: How the student handled the diversion — quality of decision-making, heading/fuel calculations, and communication when the plan changed
reveal_topics: Why GPS Killed Pilotage Skills — Before GPS, pilots constantly scanned for checkpoints, compared chart to ground, maintained situational awareness. After GPS: 'magenta line' flying, heads-down, loss of awareness.
Case (2021, Military GPS Jamming): Civilian pilots near test area lost GPS, many declared emergencies, unable to navigate, several diverted uncertain of position.
Lesson: GPS is a tool, not a crutch. Always maintain pilotage skills.
Advanced Concept: Military pilots practice GPS-denied navigation (inertial, TACAN). Consider practicing XC with GPS turned off to maintain proficiency.

concepts.instructional_intent: Response to deteriorating destination weather: decide to divert, measure/estimate heading (chart/GPS), calculate distance/time/fuel, communicate with ATC, execute. Quick diversion method: estimate heading visually, turn, refine with landmarks, confirm with GPS/VOR.

If uncertain: climb, circle, check VOR (tune nearest, identify radial), contact ATC 121.5 MHz, confess ('I am a student pilot and uncertain of my position'), squawk 7700 if critical. ATC will ask: last position, heading, airspeed, altitude, fuel. ATC provides: radar vectors, weather, frequency.

Monitor every 15 minutes, compare to plan. If consumption higher → divert early. Fuel totalizer (if equipped) more accurate than float gauges. Switching tanks every 30 min for balance. Leaning above 3,000 MSL reduces burn 10-15%. Never switch tanks during critical phases.

Flight following: ATC tracks on radar, provides traffic advisories, free service. Position reports format. Changing frequencies (handoff procedure). Request: 'Boston Approach, Skyhawk 2177U, request flight following.'

Preparation: review Chart Supplement (runway, pattern, CTAF, FBO), check NOTAMs, overfly at pattern altitude + 500 to identify runway/windsock/traffic. Entry: standard 45° to downwind with radio announcement. After landing: transient parking, secure aircraft, close flight plan.

student_view.objective: Solo cross-country flight (KHMP → KBID → KACK → KHMP) with CFI endorsement. Post-flight: checkride preparation and oral exam review.
must_do_actions: Obtain required solo XC endorsements (pre-solo XC training 61.93(c)(1), solo XC make/model, route-specific first-time)
Execute solo cross-country flight (150 NM total, 3 full-stop landings, one leg >50 NM)
Demonstrate all Private Pilot ACS task areas
Review oral exam topics after flight (certificates/documents ARROW, airworthiness inspections, weather, performance, regulations, aerodynamics, systems)
Review flight test maneuvers and ACS tolerances (altitude ±100 ft, heading ±10°, airspeed ±10 knots, bank ±5° in steep turns)
Identify remaining weaknesses and create study plan
target_numbers: Solo XC completion (150 NM, 3 full-stops, one leg >50 NM)
Flight test maneuver proficiency to ACS standards
Weakness identification and study plan creation

reveal.primary_focus: Celebrating the student's achievement while grounding expectations — the Private Pilot license is a license to learn, not proof of mastery
reveal_topics: Why the Checkride Is Just the Beginning — Private Pilot = License to Learn. NTSB data: highest accident rate is 50-200 hours total time (post-private, pre-commercial).
Why? Overconfidence ('I passed, I'm great'), complacency (stop studying/practicing), new challenges (first passengers, first XC alone, first IMC encounter).
'Killing Zone' (50-350 hours): most dangerous period for GA pilots. Accidents spike (fuel exhaustion, VFR into IMC, stall/spin).
Mitigation: humility (checkride = minimum standard, not mastery), mentorship (fly with experienced pilots), conservatism (don't push limits early).
Advanced Concept: Airlines require 1,500 hours for ATP. Even with Private Pilot, you're a beginner. Treat every flight as a learning opportunity.

concepts.instructional_intent: Endorsements required: pre-solo XC training (61.93(c)(1)), solo XC (make/model specific), route-specific (first time). Limitations: 50 NM minimum from departure, full-stop at each airport, recommended flight plan, weather per CFI discretion. Long solo XC for Private Pilot: 150 NM total, 3 full-stop, one leg >50 NM.

Two parts: Oral Exam (~2 hr, knowledge) and Flight Test (~1.5 hr, skill). Oral topics: certificates/documents (ARROW), airworthiness, weather, performance, regulations, aerodynamics, systems. Flight maneuvers: preflight, taxi, runup, normal/crosswind takeoff, slow flight, stalls, steep turns, ground reference, navigation, emergencies, landing.

Top 5 failure items: slow flight (altitude +100/-0), steep turns (rollout ±10° of entry heading), soft-field takeoff (premature liftoff), diversion (poor heading/fuel estimate), airspace (can't identify on chart). Mitigation: practice to ACS standards, memorize V-speeds, study airspace, know systems cold.

Private Pilot privileges (carry passengers, share expenses) and limitations (no compensation). Next ratings: Instrument, Commercial, Multi-Engine, CFI. Continuing education: WINGS program, Flight Review (24 months per 14 CFR 61.56), Rusty Pilots Program.

Currency ≠ proficiency. Currency = legal minimums, proficiency = actual skill. Stay proficient: fly regularly (monthly), practice emergencies with CFI, fly with other pilots, take recurrent training.
